title: Block Cipher Modes
subtitle: ECB, CBC, CTR, and why mode choice matters

content.text: The same block cipher (AES) can operate in different modes. The mode determines how blocks are chained and what security properties you get.

content.code:
ECB (Electronic Codebook)
  - Each block encrypted independently
  - NEVER USE: identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks
  - Leaks patterns (famous "ECB penguin" image)

CBC (Cipher Block Chaining)
  - Each block XORed with previous ciphertext before encryption
  - Needs random IV; vulnerable to padding oracle if used with PKCS7

CTR (Counter)
  - Turns block cipher into stream cipher using a counter nonce
  - Parallelisable; no padding needed

GCM (Galois/Counter Mode)
  - CTR + authentication tag
  - RECOMMENDED for new applications

content.text: Use AES-GCM for all new applications. It provides both confidentiality and integrity.

questions.question: Why should you never use ECB mode?
options: Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, leaking patterns
questions.explanation: ECB mode encrypts each block independently, so identical plaintext blocks always produce identical ciphertext, revealing structure.

faq.q: What is a padding oracle attack?
faq.a: An attack on AES-CBC where an attacker modifies ciphertext and observes whether the server returns a "padding error", allowing decryption of arbitrary ciphertext byte by byte.

examples: Migrating from AES-CBC to AES-GCM in a REST API
